headline: Augusta water district sues five paper-industry defendants over PFAS cleanup costs
dek: The Greater Augusta Utility District wants upstream manufacturers to help pay for treating contamination that forced the shutdown of Riverside wells and a $2 million filtration project.
body: The Greater Augusta Utility District has filed a federal lawsuit seeking to shift the cost of PFAS treatment from its customers and taxpayers to companies it says contributed to contamination in the Kennebec River watershed. The complaint, filed Oct. 7 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine, names Sappi North America Inc., Huhtamaki Inc., Kimberly-Clark Corporation, American Tissue Corporation and American Tissue Mills of Maine LLC as defendants. The public docket identifies the case as an environmental matter under the federal law commonly known as Superfund, but it does not establish that any defendant is liable.

The district’s claim follows a major change in Augusta’s water system. Testing at the Riverside well complex on Nov. 4, 2024, found a combined 23.3 parts per trillion of six PFAS compounds, above Maine’s interim 20-parts-per-trillion standard. The district’s published results show the total came from multiple compounds, including PFOA, PFOS, PFHxS and PFHpA. The [Greater Augusta Utility District’s PFAS records](https://www.greateraugustautilitydistrict.org/pfas) show the Riverside wells had measured 8.53 parts per trillion in March 2023, illustrating why the later result prompted a more urgent response.

Officials shut the Riverside wells and supplied east-side customers from wells near Bond Brook while the district designed and installed treatment. Independent reporting by [the Kennebec Journal](https://www.centralmaine.com/2026/10/09/greater-augusta-utility-district-completes-2-million-pfas-filtration-project/) said the new system cost about $2 million and was supported by a grant from the Maine Drinking Water Program. The filtration system began sending treated water back into the system this summer. The district serves about 13,750 customers, according to [the Portland Press Herald](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/10/13/augusta-utility-sues-4-paper-mills-over-toxic-pfas-in-drinking-water/).

The lawsuit targets companies connected to paper and packaging manufacturing rather than only the chemical producers most often named in national PFAS litigation. The Press Herald reported that the defendants’ facilities made or handled grease-resistant paper and disposable food products, with operations historically located along the Kennebec corridor in Skowhegan, Waterville, Winslow and Augusta. The district alleges that releases from multiple facilities combined over time. That is an allegation in a newly filed complaint, not a court finding, and the defendants will have an opportunity to contest both the factual claims and the legal theory.

The watershed makes the case more complicated than a claim tied to one isolated disposal site. The reporting describes a roughly 30-mile river corridor where pollutants from multiple sources may have mixed before reaching groundwater connected to the Riverside wells. The district points to state testing of water, landfill leachate and fish tissue as part of the evidence it plans to use. The utility has also acknowledged that it cannot identify one definitive source for the increase, a question that could become central as the lawsuit develops.

Maine’s environmental rules provide important context. The [Maine Department of Environmental Protection](https://www.maine.gov/dep/spills/topics/pfas/index.html) describes PFAS as a large class of persistent, human-made chemicals historically used in products including heat-resistant food packaging. The agency says Maine’s interim standard for six PFAS compounds remains 20 parts per trillion until April 26, 2027, while public water systems are on a longer schedule for full compliance with amended drinking-water rules. Those standards explain the regulatory trigger for Augusta’s response, but they do not decide who should pay for the district’s treatment system.

The utility’s legal strategy could matter beyond Augusta if other public water systems pursue manufacturers whose historical operations affected shared watersheds. The Press Herald reported that Maine has no complete historical record of industrial PFAS discharges into public waters, making source attribution difficult even as the state now requires monitoring and reporting. In the Augusta case, the court will have to sort through the district’s evidence, the defendants’ responses and the application of federal cleanup law before any responsibility or reimbursement is determined.

For now, the immediate public-health problem is being managed through treatment rather than a return to the untreated Riverside supply. The court docket records the complaint and summonses, with a Jan. 5, 2027 deadline for service of process. The next stages will include responses from the named companies and the court’s handling of the district’s claims. Until those steps occur, the lawsuit is a request for cost recovery—not a judgment that the paper-industry defendants caused the contamination or owe a particular amount.
